message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference to Its Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | ¹H ≈ 99.98 %, ²H ≈ 0.02 %, ³H negligible |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first ionization) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, so H⁻ is unstable in free space) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | ~53 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| **Physical State (Room Temperature)** | State | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| | Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat (gas, 1 bar) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Thermal conductivity | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound | ~1270 m s⁻¹ |
| | Refractive index | 1.000132 (visible light) |
| **Chemical Behavior** | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds; diatomic H₂ is the most stable form |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (e.g., H⁺), –1 (e.g., H⁻) |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a proton donor (acid) or acceptor (base) depending on context |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive with halogens, oxygen, and many metals; forms hydrides |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (low) |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Variable; generally soluble in nonpolar solvents |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, heavier isotope; used in NMR, D₂O (“heavy water”) |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay, T½ ≈ 12.32 y); used in nuclear fusion research |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Nuclear spin | ½ (¹H), 1 (²H), ½ (³H) |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.7928 µ_N (¹H), 0 (²H), –1.913 µ_N (³H) |
| | Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) | ¹H NMR is the most common NMR technique |
| **Astrophysical & Energy Applications** | Stellar fusion | 4 p → ⁴He + 2 e⁺ + 2 ν_e (pp chain) |
| | Fusion fuel | D–T (deuterium–tritium) fusion is the most studied reaction |
| | Energy density | 141 MJ kg⁻¹ (theoretical, if all H is converted to He) |
| | Hydrogen economy | Fuel cells (PEMFC, SOFC), hydrogen storage (compressed gas, liquid, metal hydrides) |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; lower explosive limit (LEL) ≈ 4 % (v/v) in air |
| | Explosion risk | Requires careful venting and leak detection |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but can cause asphyxiation in confined spaces |
| | Storage | Compressed gas (up to 700 bar), cryogenic liquid (–253 °C), metal hydrides, chemical carriers (e.g., ammonia borane) |
| **Miscellaneous** | Spectral lines | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) |
| | Quantum mechanical significance | Hydrogen atom is the prototypical system solved exactly in quantum mechanics |
| | Historical note | First element discovered by Henry Cavendish (1776); named by Antoine Lavoisier (1789) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and (in its most common form) one neutron.
- **It exists mainly as diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but its isotopes and ions play crucial roles in chemistry, physics, and energy research.
- **Its low density and high reactivity** make it ideal for fuel cells and rocket propellants, but also require stringent safety protocols.
- **In stars, hydrogen fusion powers the Sun** and other stars, converting mass into energy via the E=mc² process.

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any of these categories—whether you’re curious about hydrogen’s role in fusion reactors, its spectroscopic fingerprints, or its behavior in extreme environments!
